title: Man. Post. Cap. IV: PLAC — silentium minoris; syllogismus
pass_a_gloss: PLAC. That he does not move a dispute about the major here he does prudently: for besides those three reasons which follow in the Manuscript, to which he answered nothing, violation of the condition or precept first cannot be the penalty of an antecedent sin, since it is the first sin, nor of itself, since it cannot be later than itself: and ridiculously would a threat be attached to a precept which threatened that the precept would be violated if it were violated. The minor I had confirmed by an argument which it seemed safer to him to cover with silence than to touch. It can also be proved thus. Sin is violation of the law. Privation of justice in a man is sin. Therefore privation of justice is violation of the law. What clearer? But he distinguishes privation of justice into active and passive: that by which the man himself by acting badly strips himself of justice, this by which God deprives the man of justice: that he confesses to be violation of the law, this he denies. From which it follows that this, not that, was the law threatened to its violator. Let us therefore consider that distinction a little more attentively. Rightly indeed privation of justice is called active with respect to the man privating himself of justice: for active is said with respect to the agent. But passive — why is it not similarly said with respect to the privated or patient man? For as the privating answers to the privated, agent to patient, action to passion, so active privation seems to be of the privating, passive truly of the privated? Why then is the passive attributed to God, who deprives the man of justice, is not himself privated in any way? This first.
pass_b_english: Placeus. He is wise not to fight the major here. Besides three further Manuscript reasons he never answered, the first breach of the condition cannot be the penalty of some earlier sin—because it is the first sin—nor the penalty of itself, since nothing is later than itself. It would be absurd to attach to a precept a threat that the precept will be broken if it is broken. I had already confirmed the minor by an argument he preferred to bury in silence rather than face. Another proof: sin is law-breaking; privation of righteousness in a man is sin; therefore that privation is law-breaking. Clearer still? Yet he splits privation into active and passive—the man's self-stripping versus God's stripping—and admits only the first as law-breaking. So on his view the threatened law-penalty is the second, not the first. Look harder at that split. "Active" rightly names privation from the agent's side—the man who strips himself. Why then is "passive" not named from the patient's side—the man stripped? Privating answers to privated, agent to patient, action to passion; so active privation belongs to the one who strips, passive to the one stripped. How then is the "passive" assigned to God, who strips the man and is never himself stripped? That is the first point.
source_text: PLAC. Quod de majore litem hic non movet, prudenter facit: nam praeter tres illas rationes, quae sequuntur in Manuscripto, ad quas nihil respondit, violatio conditionis seu praecepti prima nec antecedentis peccati poena esse potest, cum sit peccatum primum, nec sui ipsius, cum non possit posterior esse seipsa: & ridicule apponeretur praecepto comminatio, quae minaretur fore ut violetur praeceptum, si violetur. Minorem argumento confirmaveram, quod illi visum est tutius silentio tegere, quam attingere. Potest etiam sic probari. Peccatum est violatio legis. Privatio justitiae in homine, est peccatum. Ergo privatio justitiae est violatio legis. Quid clarius? At ille distinguit privationem justitiae in activam & passivam: illam qua homo ipse male agendo justitia seipsum spoliat, hanc qua Deus hominem justitia privat: illam fatetur esse violationem legis, hanc negat. Ex quo sequitur, hanc, non illam, legem esse suo violatori comminatam. Consideremus igitur paulo attentius illam distinctionem. Recte sane privatio justitiae activa dicitur respectu privantis se justitia hominis: activa enim dicitur respectu agentis. Sed passiva, cur non similiter dicitur respectu privati seu patientis hominis? Nam ut privans respondet privato, agens patienti, actio passioni, ita videtur privatio active sumpta esse privantis, passive vero privati? Cur ergo passiva tribuitur Deo, qui privat hominem justitia, non privatur ullo modo? Hoc primum.

choices.choice: Silence safer than touching minor; critique God-as-passive
